catalog_quote: Stress in the Gilaki language is dynamic. In words not having inflectional, morphological endings, it falls on the last syllable: (12) a. xånə́ house b. kårəgə́r worker c. šenǻ swimming. In the situation where the case enclitic -ə of the genitive case, -a of the accusative case, or the “Ezafe” enclitic -ə joins to the noun, the stress remains on the stem: (13) a. mi pérə xånə my father’s house b. u duxtə́ra bavər bring this girl c. fíkrə Məryəm the thought of Maryam. In a verb in the forms of the aorist, the present-future tense and the imperative mood, the stress falls on the end of the word, that is, on the personal ending: (14) a. bəgə́m (if) I say b. kunə́m I am doing, I shall do c. bukún do! new_statements.rule_in_words: Dynamic (expiratory) word stress on the final syllable of the uninflected word (stem-final); case and ezafe enclitics, the indefinite -i and the enclitic copula are outside the stress domain, so stress stays on the last stem syllable. Verbs are morphologically conditioned: personal endings carry stress in aorist/present-future/imperative, the negative prefix nV- always attracts stress, and past neutral/past continuous forms keep stress on the stem (not on bə- or the ending).
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (genitive -ə, accusative -a, ezafe -ə) unstressed; vocative use of nouns shifts stress to the first syllable (bə́rara 'O my brother'); negative particle stressed (nə́-gəm, nú-kun); past tenses stem-stressed (bəgóftə); enclitic copula unstressed but negative copula ní- stressed (p. 132). Stilo (EIr. 2001) adds lexical/morphological minimal pairs (xaná 'legible' vs xána 'the khan-OBJ', bídin 'see!' vs bidín 'irreligious') and notes Eastern Gilaki (Lahijani) has more initial-stressed verb forms, with bV- stressed in all tenses.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; rule stated for citation forms of uninflected words, with morphological conditioning in inflected nouns and verbs. Description based on the speech of Rasht (Western Gilaki) informants.
new_statements.identity_note: Rastorgueva et al. describe the Gilaki of the city of Rasht (Western Gilaki, 'Rashti'), based on Rasht-born informants in Moscow and Rashti texts; Glottolog treats Rashti as a dialect under gila1241. Stilo (EIr.) notes that Eastern Gilaki (Lahijani) differs mainly in verb stress (more initial-stressed verb forms, bV- stressed in all tenses) while 'other stress rules are common to all dialects', so the final-stress rule for nouns/uninflected words holds language-wide.

sources.note: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 19: stress is dynamic; in words without inflectional endings it falls on the last syllable (xåne´, kårəgə´r, šenå´); case/ezafe enclitics (-ə, -a) do not take stress (stress stays on stem); aorist/present-future/imperative verbs stress the personal ending; negative particle nə-/nu-/ni- attracts stress; past neutral and past continuous keep stress on the stem (bəgóftə, góftim). Elsewhere: vocative nouns shift stress to the first syllable (p. ~65); enclitic copula unstressed, negative copula stressed on ní- (p. 132).

sources.citation: Stilo, Donald. 2001. GILAN x. Languages. Encyclopaedia Iranica, Vol. X, Fasc. 6, pp. 660-668 (online edition, last updated 25 Nov 2013).
sources.note: Paragraph 'Stress.': 'Stress is mostly syllable-final, but some morphemes, particularly in verb forms, require stress shifts' (xayə´m 'I want', nə´xayəm 'I don't want', bəxástidi...); more Eastern Gilaki verb forms take initial stress than Western Gilaki; negation nV´- obligatorily stressed; WG bV- stressed in subjunctive/imperative, unstressed in past/perfect; EG bV- stressed in all forms; lists minimal stress contrasts (xaná 'legible' vs xána 'the khan (obj.)', ruzí vs rúzi, bídin 'see!' vs bidín 'irreligious'); indefinite -i and object marker -(y)a/-ra unstressed.
